title: Beyond the real estate: Why operational control matters in hotel investing
summary: Learn why operational control is important as European hotel investors focus on active asset management and operational growth.
body_markdown:
The investment case for a hotel extends well beyond the underlying real estate.


Hotels are operating businesses. Who operates a property, which brand it carries, how space is used, and the contractual rights an owner holds can all influence what an investor can do with an asset.


Those considerations are becoming more important as the hotel investment thesis evolves. With financing costs still well above the zero-rate era, investors are relying more on operational growth and active asset management than on cap-rate compression to generate returns.


That changes the questions investors need to ask. Identifying potential upside is one thing; having the operational and contractual flexibility to pursue it is another.


## Finding the gap between current and potential performance


Some of the most interesting hotel investment opportunities can emerge when an asset's current positioning does not align with its potential.


The issue could be the operator, the level of service, or an imbalance between revenue and costs. In other cases, the physical property may present opportunities that the current ownership has not pursued.


The reasons for a sale can also create an opening for a new business plan. An owner may have completed its original strategy, reached the end of a fund's life, encountered a refinancing event, faced upcoming capital expenditure, or simply needed liquidity for other priorities.


For the next investor, the starting point is different. The question becomes whether another phase of value creation exists and what needs to change to pursue it. This is where operational control becomes part of the investment thesis.


## Operational control starts with the contract


An investor may see an opportunity to reposition a hotel, but the property's operating agreements can determine how much freedom the new owner actually has to execute that strategy.


Hotel management agreements (HMAs), for example, establish the relationship between an owner and operator. Their provisions can address matters such as the agreement term, owner approval rights, operator performance requirements, capital expenditures, and the circumstances under which an agreement can be terminated.


Those details can have important implications for an investor's business plan. An owner considering an operator change needs to understand whether, and under what circumstances, the existing agreement can be terminated. An investor planning significant capital expenditure needs to know what rights and obligations exist around those decisions. And an investor considering the eventual sale of the asset needs to understand what happens to the operating agreement when ownership changes.


Vacant possession can provide another degree of flexibility. Acquiring a hotel without an existing long-term operator commitment can give an incoming owner more freedom to select an operator or pursue a different positioning, subject to the property's specific circumstances.


The important point is not that one operating structure is inherently better than another. The structure needs to align with the investor's intended business plan.


## Operator and brand can be separate decisions


The operator is only one part of that equation. Depending on the property's structure, an owner may also need to decide about brand affiliation. Under a franchise arrangement, the hotel can operate under an established brand while a separate company manages day-to-day operations.


Separating those functions can give owners another way to think about the asset. The question is no longer necessarily whether to keep or replace a single operator-brand combination. An investor may be able to consider the appropriate brand and the appropriate operating partner as distinct elements of the strategy. This is particularly relevant when an asset is poorly positioned to capture its potential share of demand.


A change in brand, operator, or service level will not automatically improve performance. But when an investor has identified a mismatch between the existing proposition and the market opportunity, the ability to alter those elements can provide a path for repositioning.


## The opportunity can extend to the physical asset


Operational control can also affect how an investor thinks about the property itself.


F&B is one example. Restaurants, bars, and other F&B spaces occupy valuable real estate within a hotel and contribute to both the guest experience and the property's operating model. Where the existing offering no longer supports the desired positioning or economics, an owner with sufficient flexibility may consider reprogramming those spaces as part of a broader business plan.


In other cases, investors may identify opportunities to add keys. Increasing room count can change an existing property's economics, although feasibility depends on the physical asset, planning requirements, capital costs, and market demand.


Some properties may also present an opportunity to introduce residences alongside the hotel. This can create a different product within a[hospitality](https://www.walkerdunlop.com/specialties-sectors/hospitality) -led development and expand the asset's potential uses.


These strategies are not interchangeable, nor will they make sense for every hotel. What connects them is the ability to move beyond the property's existing configuration when the market, asset, and investment strategy support doing so.


## Control matters at acquisition and exit


Operational flexibility can also influence the options available when the asset returns to market.


A prospective buyer will have its own investment thesis. Some may value an established operator and brand relationship that they can continue. Others may be looking specifically for the ability to implement a new operating strategy.


That makes it important to understand how an HMA, franchise agreement, or other operating arrangement will affect a future transaction. Provisions governing termination, transfer, and change of ownership can influence the choices available to both the current owner and the next investor.


The same principle applies at acquisition. Investors need to consider which elements of the existing business plan they can change.


## The ability to execute the investment thesis


Operational control is not a value-creation strategy on its own.


Changing an operator, repositioning a brand, reprogramming F&B, adding keys, or introducing residences only creates an opportunity when the change addresses a specific issue or unlocks an identifiable advantage within the asset.


As hotel investors focus increasingly on operational growth and active asset management, underwriting the opportunity means looking beyond what a property is today. Investors also need to understand what could change, what should change, and whether the contractual and operating structure gives them the ability to make those changes.


In that environment, the question is not simply, "Where is the upside?" It is: Do we have the control to capture it?
